Okay, ladies and gentlemen, we're about to resume our public interactive event with our next candidate, Mr. Gilbert F. Hongbo of Togo, the incumbent of the post. Thank you so much, Chair. Good morning, good afternoon, good evening to all of you. Four years ago or five years ago, I was elected. That election was a very strong choice that you made going beyond my own person by electing for the first time an African Director General, you sent a quite powerful message to the world that leadership in this institution belongs to all regions and all people. Four years later, the whole geopolitical situation, economic transformation have changed. But one thing that has not changed is the very fundamentals that led to the creation of this institution. Yet over those four years, together, we have delivered despite quite very difficult circumstances. The ILO's strength lies in its ability to come together, build a consensus around a simple truth. Without labor rights, there can be no sustainable prosperity. And without productive enterprises, there are no sustainable jobs. And without social dialogue, we cannot build consensus for change. Keeping that in mind, if entrusted with a second term, there are three things that I want to highlight in those introductory remarks, which will be part of my vision and my priorities. One is to strengthen the institution, focusing our our focus back on our mandate. And our mandate, we're talking not just about the normative action or the supervisors, but also about the four pillars of our decent work agenda, including social protection, enterprise, job, as well as social dialogue. At the same token, we need to keep in mind that our very immediate priority is the financial stability of this institution through the reform that we are going through. The second point, of course, is continuing what you have launched with the coalition for the social justice. And the third is start shaping the ILO for the future based on those transformation that I was referring to, particularly in terms of innovation, technology, and AI, where I really want to put ILO to become the international reference point when it comes to the labor dimension of artificial intelligence and the technology changes. The future belongs to countries that invest in labor rights, invest in skills, innovation and productivity. In that context, I also want to propose the creation of a very high level of experts, including our tripartite constituents, in and for us to advise this House and this body when it comes to the AI implication for the labour forces, for the world of work. So I will be presenting to you the idea of creating a high-level panel with scientists, experts, private sector to help us in this endeavour. In an increasingly polarized world, the ILO's responsibility is to build bridges, create trust, and forge common solutions. That's the leadership that I offer. Principled, pragmatic, and focused on results. Thank you, Chair.
Thank you very much. And now we're going to go ahead with the question and answer part of the dialogue. And the first representative is Mr. Matthias Tons of the employers. Over to you, please.

As you know, we as a result of that work from the specialized agency, we we come we came with this idea about expertise on demand. And of course, our unique expertise, be it on forced labor, be it on child labor, on 98, 87, 98, in terms of freedom of association, collective bargaining, the social dialogue, the social protection, informality on that domain that are quite very much respected. Listen, the discussion in the last ILC and the conclusion will certainly be guiding us, and you will see that in the upcoming in the upcoming program and budget 2829, be it in terms of the role related to gender equality in the equal pay, equal pay for work of equal value, be it in terms of care economy, be it in terms of ensuring that with this transformation in the AI, women and girls are not left behind, the implementation of 190 in terms of harassment and violence on the workplace. Thank you thank you very much well First and foremost, there's one thing I think I have to say, with all due humility, I think you have to bear in mind that when I started my career, I was trained in accountancy and throughout my career, financial management has really been what I have been involved in, financial management and crisis management. These have really been my bread and butter for many years, and I think you have to bear that in mind. I make another point. In March 2025, when donations from a significant donor were suspended, that triggered a number of results relating to staff. And we have worked on that with the World Bank. Now we want to move from that to not only assessing the vulnerability, but assessing how companies, how institution, adopt the AI and how member states adapt to the current circumstances, including at the policy level. This is one big thing for me. The second is really ensuring that we can apply AI in assisting our member states in building the labor institution, including inspection, including the labor market information system and so on. The third pillar that I'm really thinking of is the whole issue. You know, there was a lot of debate ongoing on the governance dimension and also how on a consensual basis, bringing together all the three parties we could, I think, and again, I have to be prudent, it's just a thinking that I have yet I need to mature that thinking. after maybe next cycle, very likely the SRM will have to sunset. I believe moving forward in the current transformation, in current uncertainty, we need to have a tripartite mechanism that might be able to identify possible new gaps and how we go about it. And in doing that also, it's important for us to know that, and I've said it many times, the labor productivity is going to be central. Labor productivity is going to be central. And this is on labor productivity, but you might tell me it's a global total factor productivity. And I agree, but I recognize that the investment, the capital side of the issue, maybe we have less of experience, and this is why we want to also to work with with the World Bank and others. And that connection for us is important that we also outreach. Next year, the host country, Switzerland, is going to organize the AI Summit after India this year, Korea, France, and UK. We need also outreach to see the place that we could play on that. But ILO has an important role to play when it comes to the governance labor related side of the issue. This is why in my introductory remark, I was saying that it's my plan to to propose to the GBA creation of a group of experts, you know, from the scientific, from the current AI companies, obviously, from the workers, employers, and the representative of government, so that that panel can advise the office, can advise in how do we stay on the of it when it comes to the labour dimension of AI. Thank you.
Thank you. We now go to the second question from ASPEC, which is Mr. Aminul Islam from Bangladesh, please.

Thank you, Chair. Thank you, DG, for participating. Bangladesh would like to ask this question on behalf of my group. In your assessment, what are the top three major challenges facing Asia Pacific region? And at this critical juncture, how will you ensure the challenges will be effectively addressed by ILO? Thank you.
Thank you. DG.

Listen, I think in aspect, you have to recognize, I hope you will agree with me, the region is so diverse that you know, what will be top three priority in one side of the region may not be the same three priority in another side of the region. We need to take that into account. And the level of the economic activity and development also can have big variance. We have to take that into account. Subject to that, it's clear to me that obviously the supply chain and its relation with labor clauses, the challenge that the region is having to balancing the supply chain as a wealth creator, economic growth creator, with the need to respect labor rights is one thing. A month ago, I was in a Bangkok meeting with the ASEAN Minister of Labor, and I was surprised to see that more than I was expecting, more and more countries in the region are facing the challenge of aging population. On on that. So this for me is going to be also another thing. Uh by far in large despite what I said at the beginning. I think with maybe one or two exception. I think most of countries are facing challenging in terms of labor migration. Uh on on that which also will come to me. And as we all know across Asia, Latin America, Africa, in some places in Central Asia, the informality is also a major challenge. That's what I would say. And what we are doing, and I think we have to continue doing, you might recall that since the the Singapore regional meeting and declaration that called really for a strong action from a regional dimension, which we have been implementing and we will continue implementing that. And also at the subregional or bilateral work program that I think we need to work on. On that one, it's important for me, you know, after Indonesia, G20 and India G20. Today, one thing that came up very strongly is the workforce portability, which has created a work that ongoing, I think, with India, ILO, with German funding, I think, on that. And again, you can see that in ASEAN countries, for example, the the skill recognition starting with the region is moving forward and that's why we associate ourselves with that. But clearly, when I talk about supply chain, we also have to refer to the need for skills, and for skills, particularly countries like Bangladesh and others in the region that are big exporter in the garment sector and others. So to me, And so, how do we deal with that? On one hand, you have countries that have a big exporter of labor into other countries, at the same time can face labor shortage on that. This is where I want also to focus with those countries. Thank you.
Thank you very much. We now move to the workers, and I give the floor to Ms. Kathleen Paschier, who is online. Kathleen.

Good afternoon, all, and especially our Director-General, Gilbert. Let me immediately ask you the following question. In your vision statement five years ago, you put a lot of emphasis on the importance of social justice, going back to the constitutional foundation of the organisation, which we very much welcome. This time, your vision statement is focusing on the reforms of the ILO and on driving prosperity through productivity. At a time of shrinking resources, where we have to focus on preserving the core mandate of the organization, how would you convince the workers in the world that your productivity agenda will deliver for them? And how would this be reconciled with the need to address growing inequalities, the broken social contract, and the imbalance of power in economies and labor markets between workers and employers, recognizing that the protection of workers is at the heart of the ILO, but not the promotion of business? Thank you.
Thank you. Over to you, DG.

Thank you so much, Madame Pasquier, Vice President of the Board. Clearly, I want to reiterate this what I was saying in my opening remarks. I put it the second set of priority in continuing the work we are doing in the Coalition for Social Justice. Last week, we have the annual forum online. It was very much a positive that you see that if we spend the first year trying to set it up, the platform, now we are at a point where member state institutions are using it with very growing. Today we talk about more than 400 partners and that is continuing. And it's very important to know what we're doing with the fight against inequality, as you said, with initiatives such as the cotton and the labor closest initiative that we are working with WTO, the global accelerator, which is helping moving not only social protection in the context of just a transition. So that is, and I want to be clear, is and will remain high on the agenda. When I'm talking about productivity, I think we have absolutely no choice. Productivity imposes itself in the context of AI as necessity for us to spend more time and invest more in it. But don't forget that there's also one dimension that will help fighting the inequality is the productivity, the redistribution, the distribution dimension on it. And I don't know to what extent is official or not. We heard in the month of May, I believe, the interesting challenge and solutions in the in in Korea, in the Republic of Korea with Samsung Electronics on that. So the The redistribution is an important dimension to ensure that productivity gain ultimately create more job, more quality job, but also allow the business side to reinvest in innovation and their need for capital investment. So it's something that I do know, I have to say very clearly, Madam Pasquier. I'm very much aware about the concern that each group may have. And I think if we have a very good sit down and discussion, we could come up and find the right way forward on that.
Thank you, DG. Kathleen, over to you for your second question, please.

Thank you very much, Chair. DG, the current financial constraints are forcing the ILO to downsize We have already lost many colleagues with a lot of experience and institutional memory, and more will unfortunately leave in the upcoming months. Going forward, if re-elected, how are you going to ensure the ILO's financial sustainability and safeguard its independence while protecting the core mandate and technical expertise of this House? And very specifically, how would you ensure that there would be a solid dedicated space and sufficient resources for supporting fundamental principles and especially freedom of association and the right to collective bargaining, which now also includes clearly the right to strike, according to the ICJ, in your programme and budget going forward, noting that these are the least ratified and most violated fundamental principles and rights at work. Thank you.
Thank you very much. DG.

So many issues in that one question, Madam Basquiat. Let me try to unpack on them. First of all, the financial sustainability in a very cryptic way, let me say that with the current ongoing contingency measure, we know we'll go through our biennium until December, 2027 with or without clearance of arrears. I want to be very clear. So that put me into 28-29. And in 28-29, it is my intention, you may have seen it through my PGL, the program guidance letter. Clearly for the 28-29 programming, my intention is to ask if the board agrees that the assessed contribution remains at the same level as current biennium. with the commitment of the office to cap the expenditure at 75% and therefore creating a buffer of 25%. And with that, I am sure that if I still have ideas, I will not have to leave the current situation that I have today. Third part, beyond 28, 29, I need, we need to create a mechanism that minimize. We will never be able to get to risk zero in terms of unpaid contribution, but we need to minimize the risk by building some kind of a hedge fund that will help us absorb future shocks. And for that, I want, whether we call it a resilient fund, a revolving fund, we are working right now and we'll go to the GB in November with a specific agenda item of our proposal to set up this mechanism so that we can build the medium to long term. It's very clear to me that if you are calling me a second term, by 2032, I want to make sure that I have that reserve, that hedge fund that is sufficiently built and financed. The fundamental principle and rights at work, as I said, we have absolutely no choice and there should be no debate. They will remain at the core, and this is why it was interesting when I was reviewing the outcome of the DWCP review on that. And we found that the freedom of association and the collective bargaining, a few days ago, I think there was one article Kathleen, from Jeff Vock on the collective bargaining. I wouldn't say that I agree with him on all points, but there are some points that he was raising there, which for me are quite very valid, and I'm going to take that up. And one of it is, right now, if you see the work we are doing, we are doing it from no perspective, from fundamentals or in work. So you could see that is a little bit spread. We need to have a way to really coordinate that. And this is one of the reason that we also created that unit I referred to as the policy coherence under the office of the deputy director general. in terms of collective bargaining, I think we are doing fairly well in terms of research, in terms of statistics, and we have to continue that. I think it's important to bring also in the conclusion of the ISE on the social dialogue dimension in moving forward with the preservation of the expertise on the ground that I referred to. Hopefully, we will move forward. So I can assure you the fundamentals So, from right and right work, all of that for me will be preserved.
Thank you. Uh, Kathleen, the third question from the workers, please.

There in your reforms, you're putting a lot of emphasis on decentralization and bringing more functions and resources to the field where the ILO is functioning within a broader UN framework. However, workers' experience is that often tripartism and workers' rights are not adequately recognized nor addressed in the work of the UN at field level. Many governments and employers are also not keen to include standards and comments of the ILO supervisory system in country-level priorities. How would you address these challenges if re-elected?

Thank you. I should have touched on this when we were talking about the UNHAT at the ground. And, you know, already I'm very, very so pleasantly surprised about that. Already in the last 18 months, you could see that there are much more recognition of the role of ILO and the importance of embedding the respect of labor rights in our programs through our CEB and other discussions, which is one. As part of the UN area, you have this concept of the joint knowledge hubs, and this is where one of the opportunity that I want to use in moving forward as part of the country resets. What we want to do is to ensure that our regional offices, it's a very good example when I was in Bangkok with the ESCAP and our regional director there. using our regional offices and our DWTs to much more engage with the resident coordinator on that. And as you know, this idea of having common service, common offices, of course, as part of the UN system, I want to be part of it. But I always made it very clear in our discussion with a colleague from the UNAT last month, always making clear that for ILO, Unless our social partners, the role of our social partners on the ground are recognized, not only I cannot go ahead, but I also, I said that, I also suspect my board will not close their eyes on it. So this is a fundamental element that we will need to integrate in moving forward with the country office reset in the context of the UN. The other thing for us, again, I'm coming back to one of the big thing that I want to do on the second term in working more with IFI and the regional development banks, quite frankly. It is true that sometimes we have difficulties to be heard, to be listened to, when it comes to integrating the labour dimension in the national priorities. So we also, of course, we have to continue pushing for that, but we also need to use colleagues from the work we are doing with the regional development banks. which also have the entry point in the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Commerce, and the Prime Minister's higher office, and tend to use that as well. This is why, and a typical example I referred to earlier is the ongoing work that we are doing with the IMF in the whole fiscal space and how that can help either in social protection or other dimension.
Thank you very much. Kathleen, over to you. One more time, please.

Well, very last question, a point of great concern already for a long time for workers. In recent decades, globalization has led to an increase in cross-border supply chains with precarity of work rampant, especially in the lower tiers. This issue has been difficult to address in the ILO, with notably the employers group reluctant to take joint responsibility. If re-elected, what actions would you take in this important area? What role do you see for the tripartite M&E declaration? And how do you see in this regard the outcomes of the standard setting exercise on platform workers? If elected, re-elected, I should say, what would you do to promote its ratification? Thank you.

Thank you so much, Madam Pasquier. First of all, the supply chain, I would put it this way. Practically speaking, we know that we have a decision by you, board members, for us to implement the non-normative dimension of the option we put before you and come back to 2030 and then we'll take stock. And I think this is a way to go on that. Fundamentally, I believe the issue is very simple. The supply chains are crucial for economic growth, particularly for the low-income country, middle-income countries, and also for the markets on the northern or high-income countries, let's be honest. On the flip side, nobody wants to have a supply chain with child labor, forced labor, occupational safety and health issues. And the more I talk to some small businesses or CEOs, they're really looking also for help. At the same time, they also want to make sure that, you know, they have practical concern. How do you take responsibility for what is happening at the second level, third level of of the subcontracting in your supply chain. All of those are really, it's not a denial, a practical issue that I believe together we will get there. And yes, it's of course a cross-border issue now. So my point is that, again, I'm coming back to those experiences we have with a better work of this world. I remain positive that despite the different views you refer to between workers and the employers, I remain positive that the end result, we agree to it, having supply chain functioning at the same time, free from, or where you have the minimum respect for labor right and labor clauses. And again, when I was in in Bangkok, four ministers asked us, ILO, to work with them in how do we ensure that, okay, those minimum required labour clauses are respected without, I'm quoting the expression that was used to me, without killing the supply chain itself. Promotion of 193, we are already starting it in all my trips and mission and meeting already now. It's important to know that this is a landmark for us, ILO, viewed by other multilateral system in trying to come with a way to regulate the platform and the digital economy. At the same token, the very first thing that's going to be important is how do you bring the ratify or adopt 193 at the national level in encouraging, and first of all, if I were in the government, the very first thing that I want to do, of course, is a gap analysis. to have a gap analysis done and having a work plan of how I'm going to address this gap analysis. And that's where you will see us. And again, part of our budget 28, 29, that the ratification support dimension of the output, we should have that that there. Quickly, I hope I'm not running of time, the MNE declaration next year, I think is the 50th anniversary, is my intention to use that as an opportunity to see how together again, in a consensus way, we can use that to uplift the declaration and the sustainable enterprise on one hand, respect of the labor clauses on the other side. Thank you.

Thank you very much. And thank you very much, Kathleen, on behalf of the workers. We've now completed the question and answer part of the interview. DG, you now have a maximum of five minutes for any closing remarks you'd like to make.

Thank you so much, Chair, and thanks to all of you. As a closing remark, I just want to reiterate the direction that I'm taking. If elected for a second term, I want to make sure by 2032, I really position ALO as the reference when it comes to all the ongoing transformation. We talk a lot about AI, but we also have other transformation coming from impact from the climate change, the aging population, all those. So the position I look on that is one that we're focusing on the fundamental principle and that at work, productivity, skill development. And I will not say it enough the balance between economic growth, protection, and job creation. The importance for us to support the colleague on the ground and for the implementation of our core piece of standard, but also the technical expertise in bringing AI in building the labor administration and the data collection and others dimension that they are expecting from ILO. My last point is that the current financial situation forced all of us in the UN system to look for more effectiveness. And what I really like very challenging is not just a matter of cost cutting, we said it, it forces us to see where our intervention does matter. And that forces us to really go leaner without retreating in terms of our ambition. In the current global environment, ladies and gentlemen, I'm very much convinced that we need to build an ILO that remain clear in its fundamental values, at the same token, develop enough flexibility and agility to be able to respond and adjust to the future, that there are so many uncertainties today. that is important for us to have that agility, that flexibility, while keeping our values. And for that, and for need, the further we also divergence. Even if we take all our member state, they are so divergence of views on issues, then one will say we have the traditional, the dimensions of views between workers and employers. For all of that, you need a director general. That is a bridge builder, a director general that can bring all those people, all those groups, all those views together. A director general that needs, while it may not be neutral on some of the issues, needs to keep its responsibility as an impartial leader, a leader that is not just impartial, but that is also perceived as impartial. If we truly want our number one comparative advantage, I mean, our tripartism, to be effective, that is essential. And this is exactly what I want to offer again and repeat. Pragmatism, focus on results, and preparing ILO for the future. Thank you so much.

Thank you so much, Mr. Hungbo, for sharing your vision for the future of the ILO and for engaging with us so constructively. Colleagues, we're now going to take a short break of approximately eight minutes. So we'll come back here at 4 o'clock on the dot. See you then.
